utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number, IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to move the ELMO back a little bit. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like to begin this morning by talking a little bit about your relationship to Mr. Vasiljevic. You've described your familial relationship. What I'm interested in, can you give us some idea of the contact you've had with Mr. Vasiljevic over the years? Let me begin by asking you, would you attend family functions of Mr. Vasiljevic's, Mitar Vasiljevic's family?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have already said that we are related but that it is a distant relative, and I actually don't know what degree of kinship. How far back, I don't know. We lived in relations that could be called normal, that is to say, people who belong to the same family. We didn't socialise, but we lived close by. Now, as to family functions, I did not attend -- I don't remember having been to any family function at Mr. Vasiljevic's. Perhaps I would stop by once in awhile, but not family functions. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if you were having a wedding or a baptism or other function in your branch of the Vasiljevic family, would you invite Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember having invited him. I don't know. I don't think that he was ever invited to family functions in my family. I don't recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We've heard a fair bit at this trial regarding the Serbian custom of the kum relationship, and I would ask you: Can you tell us the names of the families that you are involved in a kum relationship with?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, kum relationships and the institution of kum is something which functions in the Orthodox faith as a kum to the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, we've heard quite a bit about the kum relationship. What I'm most interested in is what families are you in a kum relationship with?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was going to tell you. All the Vasiljevics are kums with the Lukic family, but the level of kinship, if I can put it that way, if I can define it that way, is not the same between each of the Vasiljevic families with the Lukic family, depending on the development of the families, how they multiply on the Lukic side. The same thing happened on the Vasiljevic side. So one of the Lukics takes over one of the Vasiljevics, and they need not have the same kums. So that if you're looking at the complete families, then the overall clans or families of the Vasiljevic were kums to the Lukic family, but those relationships of kinship do not have the importance, in general terms, that the direct kumship relationships that two individual families have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you have --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm being clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask this follow-up question: Do you have a relationship of direct kumship with any of the Lukics?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, with the family -- with the Lukic family, the Djordje Lukic family. That man or rather, my kum, christened -- took part in my christening, and that is the family we have direct kum relationships with. He is my kum. I can't put it better than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you explain what relationship Djordje Lukic is between Sredoje Lukic is? What is the relationship between those two people?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djordje Lukezic the father of Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what would be the relationship between Djordje Lukic and Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there is some degree of kinship there, but I don't know what exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going that you once again look at D26. That's the brown ledger of the period between April and July of 1992, and I'm going to ask that you open it up to the 14th of June. I believe the ordinal number was 5353. Do you have the page open to the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found it yet, I'm afraid. The 14th of June, 5353. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you just to cast your eye over all of the patients of the 14th of June, and can you tell us, are any of the names of those patients recognisable as, or identifiable, as Muslim names?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is number 5342, and the name is Bufic Mirsada, and it refers to the 14th of June, 1992. The surname belongs to the Serb group of surnames, whereas Mirsada is a Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Other than that person, are there any other clearly identifiable names of Muslims on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either I haven't seen all the names properly, but I don't think there is another name like that for the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you now just to flip to the first day of that ledger and I'd ask you to do the same thing. Can you look over the names on the first day of that ledger sometime in April and tell us if there are clearly identifiable Muslims being treated on that day?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On page 1, there are some, quite a few Muslim names, in fact. I can say with certainty that they are Muslim names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you explain to us or what accounts for the difference between the Muslims that were treated in April and the lack of Muslims being treated on the 14th? Is there an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Muslims had, for the most part, largely left Visegrad approximately in this period, up to the 14th of June or a little later, a little after that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You mean left or were forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me when I say that nobody in the health centre told me anything about this. The Muslims that came to the health centre didn't say whether they had been forced to leave or whether they had just left of their own accord. They were looking for safety, and they were trying to get away from all the problems that had occurred at that time. So I can't really say with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You told us last week, though, that throughout, before the problems in 1992 and throughout 1992 and after 1992, everybody that needed help was given assistance at the health centre regardless of their ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, before I get to my final few questions to you, I want to ask you: You were given a guarantee of safe conduct, that you would not be arrested while you came up here to testify, and my question to you is: Why did you feel that was necessary to have such a guarantee before you would come and testify before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I can say is as far as safe conduct guarantees are concerned, I didn't think about that topic at all, whether I needed it or did not need it, did not need any guarantees, because I don't think there is anything, any reason for which I should be imprisoned or punished in any way. And as far as -- but as far as guarantees are concerned, also, I talked to my attorney, the attorney who asked me to testify before this Tribunal, and he did mention the possibility of having a guarantee, and so I agreed with him and said that if he considered that it was a good thing to have a guarantee, then he could request a guarantee if he thought it was necessary. Or if he didn't think so, he needn't ask for it. So I left it up to him. So to be quite frank, I don't know why he made that decision, and I didn't discuss that topic with him at any later time either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that you would have come to testify irregardless of this guarantee?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, before -- in order for me to ask my last few questions, I need to tell you a story, a true story in which you played a part, and I'm going to ask that you take a look at the following picture. I would ask that it be noted as Prosecution document number P11.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that be placed in front of the witness, not on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, this story begins the date before St. Vitus' Day, the 17th of June, 1992, when the young woman in that picture, a Muslim, walked into the police station in Visegrad. She was burnt over her entire body, her eyes were swollen shut, her hair was burnt off, and her fingers had melted together. She stood before the two Serbs in that police station and begged them to shoot her, to put her out of her misery. As one of them raised his weapon to obliged her, the other, a young man about 17 or 18, also with a gun, showing wisdom and compassion uncommon in those days, said no. And he took her to a house with four elderly Serb women, and he told her, "You'll be safe here and I'll return with a doctor." The next morning, on St. Vitus Day, he returned with a doctor. That doctor was you, Dr. Vasiljevic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this woman is concerned, I cannot recognise her, judging by the face, but it is a fact that I did see a young woman, a young female at Bikavac, not in front of the station but in front of the military command, the military headquarters, and this was sometime at the end of June. I know it was quite hot at the time. And they called me from the command of the brigade, and they claimed that they had a woman there who had received burns, and I remember very well going with a nurse - I think the nurse's name was Nurse Slavica, Slavica Papic - and that I did go to the spot and found a woman who had been burnt. Her face was all swollen, and it was impossible to identify her on the basis of this photograph, when it seems that her face has been treated when this photograph was taken. And what I can remember, and I can't say with certainty that it's the same person, but I did see a burnt female person, and I know that we gave her an injection and analgesics and ointments for her burns, salves, and I said I didn't know what I could do. I didn't dare take her to the health centre because I couldn't guarantee her safety there. I couldn't send her off to Foca because the roads were - how shall I tell you - in the war situation. They were in the war zone where there was shooting so they were completely impassable. I didn't dare send her to Uzice because the members and later on these people were defined as some sort of paramilitary formations, but as I say, they were along the roads, controlling the roads to Uzice and all the checkpoints. They controlled every single person and would remain at the checkpoints for a long time. So I didn't have anywhere to send her. We did what we could for her, and I suggested that if there was a way - and I remember this very well - that she should try to go through Medjedja was 10 kilometres upstream from Medjedja, and that was very near. So I suggested she should try to go there and continue her treatment there. But none of this happened in front of the police station, and the policeman didn't bring me. It happened in front -- at Bikavac, and I came at the control from someone from the military command there. So it was at the Bikavac military command, military headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, she says you told her four things. I wanted to ask you about each of those four things and ask if you admit or deny that you told her these things. The first thing that you told her is that she had very serious burns and she needed to be hospitalised, and without immediate medical treatment she would die. Doctor, did you tell her that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next thing she says, and I believe you've alluded to it already in your testimony, she said that you told her that she did not have permission to leave Visegrad to go to either Uzice hospital or Foca. She was not permitted to leave to get medical treatment. Did you tell her that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Absolutely not. I know that I didn't mention any permits of any kind, nor were permits important to me at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, then --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was important was that I could help her as far as I was able to at that -- in those circumstances, what I had with me. So what I did -- what I -- I did what I could do under the circumstances. The interpretation that I had brought her to the health centre and had I taken her to the health centre and had she been killed there, how would that have been interpreted? Would that have been interpreted as my participation in that? That is what prevented me from taking her to the health centre. And we had no possibility of giving her any substantial treatment in the health centre either. That is why I suggested that she try, if she at all could, to go to Medjedja, which I thought was relatively close by, two hours walking from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, she -- with regard to the Visegrad health centre, she says that you told her that you had no room for her in the Visegrad health centre. Did you tell her that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I told her that I didn't dare take her to the health centre. I couldn't take the risk of taking her there because I couldn't guarantee her safety there. So I'm thinking about it now. I said that I did not dare take her.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, let's recall for a minute something you said in response to a question Mr. Domazet asked you. The health centre, before 1992, during 1992, and after 1992, admitted absolutely everybody who had the need for treatment. That statement's not true, is it, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the health centre took in everybody who came to the health centre, and they would have accepted this woman, too, had she appeared. That would not have been in question. But let me repeat once again. I did not dare take the woman off towards the health centre because there were some strange groups of people whom had I never been able to define who they were and what they were, but they turned up. They turned up fairly frequently in the health centre and would probably take down the people present, the names of the people in the health centre. So that there was no way for me to be able to guarantee somebody's safety, and that is why I decided to take this other course, the one that I have explained to you. I said I did what I could for her under the circumstances. I gave her medicines for her. I gave her pain-killers, analgesics and a salve for her burns, and I went with her to a house in which there was a few other people at Bikavac. They were elderly persons. I think they were ill. I remember that I examined them as well and gave them some medicaments, too. I don't remember what actual medicines I gave. But the only reason this woman didn't go to the health centre was the absolute insecurity and lack of safety that she would be in, in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, Doctor, I ask my question again. Was it not true that Muslims who desperately needed medical treatment were denied medical treatment at the Visegrad health centre, for whatever reason you care to give us today? The fact remains that they were denied essential medical treatment; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Medical treatment was not denied. It was not denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, this person says the last thing you said to her before you left was that, "I cannot come back to treat you again." You gave her a shot, you gave her some pills, and you told her, "I cannot come back to treat you again." Is that not true? Did you not tell her that you did -- that not only could she not go to the Visegrad health centre but that you would not go to her to give her any further treatment. Is that not true, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying anything of that kind to this person or any other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, doctor, did you ever return to give her any other pain medication or any other type of treatment for her injuries?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that I did not go to Bikavac any more, and I had no occasion to see this woman again. Just for several months or one year or perhaps a little longer, I read her statement describing this event, and that is why I recall the event, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, you left her that day thinking that she would die; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I have told you that with the person in question, I went to a house where there were several Muslims. They were ill, too. I examined them and gave them medicines. Who these people were, I no longer remember. There were four or five people in that house, and I do know that I gave them medicines which I considered they needed at that particular time and that they stayed in the house together with that woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In fact, doctor, they --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I expected that -- I suppose that the woman had managed to go where I had suggested, because until the newspaper article appeared, I had never heard of that woman again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In fact, doctor, the people that she was with were not Muslims at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. all but Serbs that had shown some compassion to her, and she remained there for 11 days in Visegrad. Let me ask you this, doctor: Of all the injuries a human can suffer, would you agree with me that perhaps the most painful injury is that suffered by the types of burns that this person suffered?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Burns are something which cause great pain, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, can I assume that because you're a doctor, you've taken the Hippocratic oath just like doctors all around the world have taken? Have you taken such an oath?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that oath includes an obligation on your part to ease the suffering of the sick and to tend to the sick; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it was an oath just like the oath you took just before you testified here in this court, it was a promise to do something, to fulfil a duty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, can you help us to understand how you, a professional in the community of Visegrad, somebody who Muslims and Serbs alike looked up to, can you help us understand how you, a professional medical doctor, could have walked away from that woman, knowing the suffering she was in, knowing that you would not take her into the health centre, knowing she would not be able to go to a hospital outside Visegrad, and knowing you would not come back to treat her? Can you make us understand how somebody who is held in such regard could have acted in such a way towards this woman?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you the reasons. I was not able to take the woman to the health centre because there was no way I could guarantee her safety, absolutely no way. And had I not done what I could -- or, rather, it's not true that I didn't do everything that was possible, everything I could have done. Everything that was at my disposal, I gave her. And I tell you that I left her a large amount of analgesics, and I told her how to use them, and I also suggested to her that she should try to reach Medjedja or, rather, Gorazde, and evidently she did that in view of the fact that I later learnt that she had survived the war and that she is still somewhere in Bosnia to this day. But it's not true that I refused to help her. I cannot accept this. As a doctor, I could never refuse to treat anyone anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your prescription to her was to, on her own two feet, walk over the hills surrounding Visegrad, through the front lines, and through minefields to find a doctor who would be willing to treat her. That was your prescription for this patient; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only thing that was possible at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasiljevic, I will continue where Mr. Groome left off and ask you about this. You told us you were called to this woman from someone at the Bikavac headquarters. Can you tell me what they told you about this patient and how they described this woman?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that call very well considering the situation I lived through following from that call, which touched me deeply as a human being and as a doctor, because I was in a no-win situation. I was not able to do what I thought I should do and what I thought any doctor and any human being should do. That is why it sticks in my memory, everything about the call that came from the headquarters at Bikavac. I responded, and they told me that there was a woman in the headquarters who had been burnt. The expression "to be burnt," implies a smaller burn, something that is bearable. They didn't tell me what sort of woman this was. I had no idea who she was, and it didn't matter to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vasiljevic, does your reply mean that you did not expect the severity of the burns you found?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. According to the way people speak, especially lay people, when they describe burns as extreme as this, they speak in an excited voice. They demand that the doctor should come as quickly as possible. So you can evaluate the severity of the situation by the tone of the voice used and the words used when you're called on, but whoever called me from the headquarters spoke in a way that did not lead me to conclude this was a severe injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember, Dr. Vasiljevic, what condition you found the woman in after this phone call?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we found this lady. I don't know to what extent the Bikavac motel in which the headquarters was is familiar to the people here, but in front of the entrance -- in front of one of the entrances to the motel, there was a kind of parking lot or a playing field, whatever it was. It was a large area covered in concrete, and at the end of it there was a ramp. And I remember very well that there were two guards at the ramp, and we approached them in our car and asked them, "Where is this woman who has been burnt, the woman who needs help?" And they said, "Well, here she is. You've just passed her by." And then I turned round, and about a metre or two behind me, to my right, this woman was standing, and I cannot recognise her in the photograph here. I cannot say with certainty that this is the same woman, because her face was all swollen and she looked different. So it's practically impossible to recognise her today from a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One of Mr. Groome's questions was whether you told that woman that there was no room in the health centre. You have denied it. But my question is: Are there beds in the health centre, places where patients can be hospitalised? Was the health centre an institution in which people could be hospitalised?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in general, health centres belong to the primary level of health care and do not provide for hospitalisation. Before the war, however, we did have a certain number of beds there. I don't know why people were hospitalised there except that perhaps it was because of the power plant that was being constructed. And during the war, we still had a certain number of beds which were there for people who were not very seriously injured. However, I cannot remember whether those beds were still there at the point of time we are talking about now. So what I can tell you is that in the health centre, officially, there were no beds for hospitalisation. No patients were taken in who needed to be hospitalised. Patients were only taken in for outpatient treatment, and those who were seriously ill were transported towards Uzice. Because of the large number of wounded people, we did set up several beds in a room where people who had only been grazed by bullets could be kept, and we tried to treat them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You described this kind of medical treatment you gave her. My question is: Was there anything else that could have been done even if you had taken her to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe something more could have been done, but not much more, because the health centre did not have large quantities of medicines or bandages. However, the treatment might have been a little more efficient if we had been in the health centre. But I have told you the reasons why I dared not even consider taking her to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vasiljevic, you told us why you thought this would have been dangerous. You told us there were many paramilitaries everywhere, on the roads. Was that the main reason why you did not dare take her with you, or did you consider that the help you had given her was all that you could do?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The presence of the paramilitaries and the bands rampaging around town and in the health centre, where they came often, sometimes as many as two or three times a day, this was the only reason why this woman was not taken to the health centre. And any other statement about this is absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My last question about this is: Do you still feel that you have given her all the assistance you were able to provide at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do feel that I did everything I could have done. There was nothing else that could have helped her and that I could have done. Had I taken her to the health centre, today I might be held responsible for her possible death.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vasiljevic, one of Mr. Groome's questions was actually a statement to the effect that Muslims were not treated at that health centre in that period. You denied it, and you explained why there were few of them. My question is, because you can tell from persons' names what ethnicity they were, would Muniba Medjuseljac be a Muslim or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to her first and last name, she is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Could you tell us what date you found that name?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Just now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasiljevic, would you please look at Exhibit D26. Look at the number first, because it's easier to find than the date because of the way the records were kept. Would you look at 5558, please. So three fives and an eight.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muniba Medjuseljac, born in 1952 in Visegrad. She came to be examined with her health card, and the number is inscribed here. I can't tell exactly what number refers to what. One is the number under which she was registered at the health insurance. The other refers to the company she worked in and so on. And judging by the diagnosis, this was a sort of cancer. The code is 169. We've abandoned these codes, so I no longer remember exactly what the diagnosis was. And she was given a medicine called Valorun [phoen], which is a pill of morphine origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do we really need this sort of detail? The point was -- well, the point that was sought to be made was there were no Muslims there. If you can point out some Muslim names, do that, but we really don't want to know how they were treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So, Doctor, you need not go into detail. Would you please just look at the date and tell us the date when this person was seen?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 22nd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please now go to number 5622. Did the same person come for a check-up again, and would you tell us the date?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 5622, yes. It's the same name, Muniba Medjuseljac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please tell us the date, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date was the 24th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And one more. Would you please look at 5709?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 5709, it's the same name, Muniba Medjuseljac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please tell us the date of this last entry?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was on the 29th of June. 1992, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please go back to the 14th of June, 5353. And this refers to Mr. Groome's question, the date when Mitar Knezevic was treated.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 5353, that's Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. But under this date, Mr. Groome asked you on Friday to look at number 5332. This is the first number where the date is the 14th of June. Would you go back two pages, please. If you remember, his question was whether this number referred to a name that had been changed, the last name. The name is Sredoje, and it hasn't been altered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Mr. Groome asked you to look at the last name carefully and to say whether before it was altered it might have been a different last name, and after studying it carefully, you said it was possible that the last name under this was Lukic. Do you remember saying that on Friday?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So the last name that was Lukic has been altered. On the basis of the information you have, please tell us the date of birth of this patient which has been entered in the proper column.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's evidently an elderly man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you look at the number of the person's health file and the number that's supposed to be the index number, the one that begin with 050.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the entire number.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the number of the person's personal identity card and it refers to the date of birth. The first digits refer to the date of birth, which was the 5th of February, 1927.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the number. If it's important -- that's the index number. If it's important, you better get it recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, please read the entire personal identification number slowly and then explain what follows from this number. When you read the number, wait for the interpreters to catch up, please. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: There is a mistake again in the transcript. Let me see. Yes. It's all right now. Yes, it's all right now. Yes, it's all right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this number, one can tell the date of birth. I can't explain the rest of the code with certainty. I think it refers to gender, and the last digit would refer to the municipality or something like that, but I'm not sure. All I know is that the first seven digits refer to the date of birth in anyone's personal identification number on the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vasiljevic, according to the first seven digits of this number, what was the date of birth of this patient?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date of birth was the 5th of February, 1927. Of course, it's 1927.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vasiljevic, could this have been Sredoje Lukic, whom you probably knew, in view of his age?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Except for the name, one couldn't say that the rest of this information refers to Sredoje Lukic, the man we've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vasiljevic, in your view, does this mean that the alteration of the last name was simply a correction of a mistake made by the person who entered the name in the first place? What is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no other explanation. Here it is an improper way of correcting a mistake. It's not the way mistakes were supposed to have been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now that we are talking about this date, Mr. Groome said that on the 14th of June, and that was one of his questions on Friday, 25 patients were examined. I have counted 24, but I think the difference is not important because there is no dispute about the fact that Mitar Vasiljevic was one of the last and that there were only two names entered in after him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please look at the number or, rather, the page in front of the one we have just been discussing, 5353, and look at number 5349. Would you read us the name of the patient and what was done with this patient?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 5349 refers to Dragan Filipovic from Visegrad, a member of the Territorial Defence. And he had an injury to his left shoulder from a firearm and a superficial injury to the abdomen or, rather, the stomach, on the left-hand side, and this patient was referred to Titovo Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please count the order in which he was received that day, counting from the first patient seen on that day? Can you tell us how far down the line he was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was the eighteenth patient seen on that day. Only if I can just -- about the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, no. That was all I wanted to ask. Up until Mitar Vasiljevic's examination, only three patients were examined on the basis of this book, judging by the book. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Three patients were examined, and they were three members of the Territorial Defence. And I should like to stress that this -- this protocol refers to the Territorial Defence patients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, you recall that there is a mistake, or not a mistake but a misleading reference there to the date, because I think two pages earlier, the same date is shown. So somebody at some stage - what stage we don't know - has written that particular date again. It was certainly not the fourth person treated on that day. That was raised in cross-examination when the doctor came out with the same explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour. On page -- on the page in which Mitar Vasiljevic's name was entered, in the corner there is the second -- the 14th of June written twice. But what the witness was talking about referred to the date that appears in the first place, that is to say, after 5332, after number 5332. And that is the first examination of the day, and that was the situation with Sredoje, the case in point with Sredoje, the man that was born in 1927 that we discussed a moment ago. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So the witness counted from that patient onwards and reached Dragan Filipovic, who was number 18. And when you add three patients up to Mitar Vasiljevic, then Mitar Vasiljevic was the 22nd. And I think we can agree there that that is so and that there was no error there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vasiljevic, one of Mr. Groome's questions on Friday was the following: In view of the late examination of Mitar Vasiljevic, when could this have been? Could it have been perhaps much later on the same -- same day? That was the question. Now, I should like you to tell me the following: You do not, of course, know when the patient under number 18 was entered, Dragan Filipovic, when he arrived in Uzice. However, my question is a hypothetical one perhaps, but I have evidence about it. If Dragan Filipovic had arrived by ambulance on the 14th of June in Uzice hospital at 1540 hours, when, according to you, would you say was the latest that he was able to leave the health centre in Visegrad and to go to Uzice in view of the distance, the roads, and the circumstances of the ambulance travelling to Uzice? So if he arrived at 1540, if Dragan Filipovic who was examined under number 18 on that day arrived at Uzice hospital in the afternoon at 1540, when would he have had to leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the distance and taking into consideration the vehicles that we had at our disposal, there was a cross -- a checkpoint on the Serbian side and one on our side, and in view of the fact that they -- the ambulance would have been stopped at both those checkpoints, most probably he would have needed an hour and 15 or 20 minutes to reach Uzice. That was how long the journey usually took. And when the weather conditions were bad, then the time required to be longer. So if he arrived, you said, at 15 -- what did you say? You said 1540 hours or 1545.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I said 1540.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 1540. That would mean he might have left Visegrad an hour and 20 minutes later. No, I mean earlier. He would have had to leave Visegrad 1 hour and 20 minutes before that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vasiljevic, under the best conditions with respect to the border crossings and all the rest, you say that the journey would have taken an hour and twenty minutes. So ideally, the patient could have left sometime after 2.00 p.m. for Uzice. Does that mean that his examination was conducted before that time, that is to say, probably between 1.00 and 2.00 p.m., 1.00 and 2.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the only conclusion one can draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Vasiljevic. In answer to a question from Mr. Groome, when he asked you whether it was exact that in the protocol that you have before you that no entry was made of the time of the examination of patients, Mr. Groome on Friday indicated several cases, pointed out several cases where the time had in fact been recorded, and you confirmed that and said that that wasn't common procedure but that this could have happened. I looked through the entire protocol book and came across only six cases like that, and I think that they are the ones that you have just looked at. But I'm going to ask you to look at the first day, the 24th, where there were four cases in point, four cases like that, and could you tell us whether it was one and the same person who made those entries, and you would also tell me if the entries are made in the Cyrillic or the Latin script. The number is 2846 onwards.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have here from 284 -- 2846, 2849, we have the times of admission, which is not customary, as I said. And I don't know what made somebody record those times only for those four patients. Otherwise, the information about the patient is entered in Cyrillic up until the medical data, which is customarily written in the Latin script.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at the section before this number, before 2846, whether it is the same handwriting and the same Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The handwriting is not the same. I'm not a handwriting expert, but of course -- of course, but quite evidently it is two different handwritings and two different scripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that the case with 2849, that is, 2850 onwards?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, following on, we now have a different handwriting and it is the Latin script and not as in the previous few cases, the four cases, in fact, it was the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In those four cases, in addition to the time entries, does it also state the date? So the date and time.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Next to each one of those it gives the time and date, the 24th, 1645, 1845, and 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please leaf through the book as quickly as possible to see if there is more Cyrillic script and where the time is entered. Could you go up to the number 4063, which is five days later. Would you leaf through those pages to see if there are any other entries in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Giving it a quick look, I can note that there are no other handwritings in the Cyrillic script up until the number you mentioned, and then up until the number -- that is, up until the number 4063, the 25th of April, 1992, and 1925, the time of admission was recorded. Before that, 4062, it states the date of admission, the 25th of April, 1992, without the time. And that was entered in the Cyrillic script once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The number 4063, you state, is an entry written in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 4062 and 4063 is the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And no other entries are written on that page in the same handwriting and script; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, not one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One more check, Mr. Vasiljevic, 4130. Would you look at number 4130 and tell us whether that is the same case, that is to say, a Cyrillic recording of names and surnames and that that is the only entry with a date next to it.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 4130, there is the date and time, and the rest of the information is written in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you as far as that is concerned. I'm not going to ask you to leaf through the book any more, but from that time, until the 20th of June, there no further handwriting or Cyrillic script. It was only on the 20th of June that this occurred again, but I don't think we need to go into that now. Would you take a look at number 4388 now, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you read out the date, who the patient was and what was done.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lepenica Selim was the patient, born in 1947, from Gorazde, and he came by in passing, being transported from Gorazde to Titovo Uzice. Probably, they needed something along the way, so they stopped by at the health centre Visegrad. But he was -- the patient was being transported from Gorazde to Titovo Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasiljevic, 5630 is the next number I'd like to have you look at, and 5461.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You don't have to read everything. You have already commented on it. But were these people sent to Uzice, and were they sent there in separate ambulances or the same ambulance, if you can see that from looking at those numbers -- at that number?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the protocol, you can see that they were sent in the same ambulance to Titovo Uzice. They were dispatched in the same vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you look at 5473, a little further on, and read out who that was and whether you can identify what the intervention on that person was, what it was about, and the date, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number 5473, the entry is (redacted), from Visegrad. She came, it seems, without her health booklet, as there are no -- there is no information from her health booklet that had been entered. She seems to have come without.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you see the date and whether -- and can you see what was done in her case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 1st of June -- no, I'm sorry, the 18th of June, 1992. The 18th of June, 1992, is the date. And it says, "Applied Novogetal [phoen] injections, penicillin, Garamycin and Ultracortine [phoen], and she was bandaged, that particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. A little further on, please look at number 5483 now.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 5483, the entry is Slavko Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you read out the date and tell us whether he was referred to anywhere, looking at the protocol book, whether you can see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 18th of June, 1992, and he was sent to Titovo Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now five numbers later, 5488. Would you check that out, please, and tell us what you see?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5488, the entry is Mitar Music, 724 Novo Gito [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, perhaps I have made a mistake. See if you have Rajak Novo.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 5484 is Rajak Novo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I apologise, I got the number wrong. Would you have a look at 5484.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was dispatched to Uzice as well, referred to Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is it the same date, the 18th of June like the other case, 5483?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5483, Rajak Novo and Trifkovic Slavko. They, on the 18th of June, 1992, were referred to Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you now please take a look at 5597?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5597, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Loncarevic Goran is the entry. He is from Visegrad, and sent to the surgical unit in Uzice as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name and surname or, rather, the person?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know whether the injury was received at the front line or in Visegrad perhaps? Can you tell that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it is a colleague of mine, Loncarevic, and we worked together, I know that he sustained his injury on the premises of the health centre, when he was getting out of bed. Whether the pistol fell to the floor, I don't know exactly, but I know that the pistol went off and it was a self-inflicted injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you take a look at one more number for me, please. 5170.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 5170, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entry is Milan Lukic, the patient, born in 1967, TO. The diagnosis was written using the 491 code. He received glucose, Pedoxin, Lincosine [phoen] and Garamycin, and something else I can't decipher. He was not referred anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember what the code diagnosis 491 referred to at the time? What was that a code for?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you give us the date of the entry for that patient?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date was the 7th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And one more question for you, Mr. Vasiljevic. Do you happen to remember at that time who were the drivers who drove the ambulances of the health centre, especially for the people who were transferred to Uzice?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was Zivorad Savic, one of the drivers, and another one was Vlade -- well, I can't remember what his surname was. I do know his surname, but I just can't remember. If I do, I'll tell you. The third was Ljubo Zecevic, and the fourth, I assume, was Svetin Sikiric, but I'm not sure whether he was a driver during this particular period of time. He was later on and he's still in the health centre, but whether he was a driver at that time, I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was there a driver called Marijan at all?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was Marijan Markovic, a driver who later on was killed. I didn't remember him. But yes, Marijan Markovic was a driver who was in the health centre when the war broke out; that is to say, he had worked before the war, during the war, and a little later, until he was killed. He was a driver. And this man Sikiric had probably replaced Marijan as a driver for the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that one was a driver, and you couldn't remember Vlado's surname. Was it perhaps Vladimir Jovicic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Vladimir Jovicic, that's what he was thinking of, and he is from the village of Vardiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And mention was made on Friday, Dr. Vasiljevic, about a letter in which you explained that you signed it. You were shown an English copy, and I didn't have the B/C/S version myself. I do have one now, so I'd like to show it to you, and would you confirm whether that is the letter that you were talking about on Friday and which you signed. And I have it in sufficient copies, so I should like it tender it into evidence in addition to D11, so perhaps D11/1 B/C/S text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: D11 is not yet in evidence. But you want to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not but I would like to, yes Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm a little wary of when you say that is your last question, but we've been through two of them this morning. Is this your last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's just the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any objection to the tender of that, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't heard if the doctor recognises it. I would wait for his answer before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I thought he had answered.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it. I recognise this document. Let me say it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On that basis, I have no objection to the tendering of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The B/C/S will be D11, and the English will be D11.1. Well, doctor, thank you very much for coming along to give evidence and the give which you have given. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, for inviting me to come and state what I know about the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, it may be that I've received it and can't find it, but have we got a list of witnesses for this week yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You have a list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That is all right. It has been received but I just can't find it, but I'm going to get a copy. Very well. We'll adjourn now and we resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, madam, would you stand up, please, and make the solemn declaration on the document the usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Tomasevic, good day.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, on behalf of the Defence, I will put some questions to you. In view of the fact that we speak the same language, for the sake of interpretation, would you please make a pause of a few seconds after the end of my question before giving your reply, and I will endeavour to do the same so that both question and answer can be properly interpreted. Mrs. Tomasevic, would you please introduce yourself to us. Tell us your full name and your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Milena Tomasevic, born on the 12th of December, 1955, in the area of Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, would you tell us what your profession is.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I am the chief nurse in the psychiatric ward or, rather, in the higher medical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Am I to understand that the school you mentioned is your highest qualification?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, you are now the head nurse in the psychiatric ward of the general hospital in Uzice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: For how long have you been working in the general hospital in Uzice?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Since 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since when have you been working in the psychiatric ward of that hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. As I understand from your reply, that from 1979 until Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. today, you have been in the same ward, I will ask you to explain to us, especially with reference to the year 1992, how records on patients were kept in your ward.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The protocol was led by the chief technician or his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say the chief technician or his deputy, you are speaking in the male gender. Is that the same as the head nurse?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please wait for the end of my question. When you say the chief technician, are you referring to a man doing the same job that is usually done by a woman as the head nurse? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So in your ward, a protocol or ledger of patients was kept?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please explain to us the manner in which this protocol was kept and the data it contained?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The details for the ledger were taken from the diagnosis, the case history, which contained the following details: When the patient was received, where he came from, what his occupation was. This was all taken down when a new patient was admitted. His personal identification number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, when a patient is admitted to the general hospital and is admitted for the first time at your ward, is that the date you enter as the date of his admission to hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Tomasevic, when such a patient arrives to you from another ward, do you enter the date of his admission to the general hospital in your ledger, the date when he was admitted not to your ward but the ward where he was before he came to your ward?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We enter that date and we make a note as to when the patient was transferred to our ward, in the form of a note or a remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, when the opposite happens and the patient is transferred from your ward to another ward of the same hospital, is that entered in the ledger?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: It is entered in the report, and it should be entered in the case history.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, do you have a ledger of patients for the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you were coming here to testify in The Hague, did you take the original protocol book with you?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is it this book which is now in my possession and which I will show to you just now, and ask you to tell us whether this is the protocol in question and from what date to what date the patients were entered into this protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher please take this book.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the protocol of patients which I have brought with me, which I took with me when I came here to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please look at the first and last page and tell us what period this book refers to.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The 4th of November, 1991. The 16th of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This book, therefore, covers all the patients at the psychiatric ward in Uzice between these two dates in 1991 and 1994. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Madam, when you set out to The Hague in order to testify, you knew you were going to testify in the Mitar Vasiljevic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does the name of Mitar Vasiljevic figure in your protocol of 1992, and if so, could you please find the relevant entry?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does figure in the ledger, under number 386, which contains details, Vasiljevic Mitar, 1954, Sandzacka 104, Visegrad, reserve soldier. Note, transferred from the orthopaedic ward on the 7th of July, 1992. And underneath -- should I read everything?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please read everything, but go in order, from the first column on, and say whether something is written in it or not. So could you read us the column headings and tell us what has been filled in.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the ordinal number is 386. The date of admission, it says here, that's the date of admission, the 14th of June, 1992. Last name and first name, Vasiljevic Mitar. Year of birth, 1954. Street and number, that is, address, Sandzacka 104, Visegrad. And where it says "Form of medical insurance," well, he was a reserve soldier in Visegrad. Then it says diagnosis, 298.9, 823.2. Where it says "therapy," this is where the number of the case history's entered. It says 10014. And then note, to who he was referred and when. It says transferred from the orthopaedic ward on the 7th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And right after this date, the 7th of July, 1992, is there another date in the same column?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is. This is the date of his release, the 28th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, when you read the ordinal number in which -- under which he was entered, 386, the next thing you read was the 14th of June, 1992, as the date of admission. Is this the date of admission in your ward or to the general hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: It refers to his admission to the general hospital in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Looking at this book, would you be able to recognise the handwriting and say who entered these details on this page, including the name and last name?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is this your handwriting in this column 386, which you read, and also in the column before and after it on this page?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: It's my handwriting, except for the diagnosis and the date of discharge. That's not my handwriting either because it was done when the patient was sent home, and this was done by the chief technician. The rest was entered by me because I was his deputy at the time. So I took down the case history and his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Looking at this page and the dates of the other entries, can you tell us when you entered these details in this book, on what date?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: This was entered only the 8th of July, because the 7th is a state holiday. So I wasn't at work on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Under the following number, 387, what is the date entered as the date of admission?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The 8th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would this mean that this patient was admitted on that date?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the previous case or, rather, the case before Mitar Vasiljevic, that is 385, what is the date of admission?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Between the two dates of admission, we have the date of admission of Mitar Vasiljevic, but the date entered next to his name is the 14th of June, which was the date he was admitted to the general hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it possible to get a photocopy of this document? I'm finding it very difficult to follow the examination of the witness. I also point out that Mrs. Tomasevic was here from last Thursday but this is now the first that I'm being told of a ledger. I would appreciate the opportunity to view some of these documents before the witness takes the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We have been through this before, Mr. Domazet. Where are the copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will hand out photocopies of the page in the ledger referred to. Unfortunately, I don't know how useful they will be because the entries are in the Cyrillic alphabet, in Cyrillic handwriting, as the witness will confirm, all the details except for the numerals. I'm willing to hand them over. I'm ready to do so. And this is the page, so would the usher please take them. It may make it easier to follow, but I'm not sure that you will be able to follow without a translation. Would you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, that may be so, but if it had been given to the Prosecution after the witness arrived with the book last week, they could have taken some steps to have the Cyrillic translated. And you really must remember that it is impossible for these cases to proceed based as they are so often on documents unless both the parties have got copies of them. Now, if you have any more of these books to produce, please give copies of them now to the Prosecution so that if they are in Cyrillic, they can get them translated. Even if they're just in ordinary B/C/S Latin words, they still must be given the opportunity of getting on with it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It was only during the break on Friday that I was able to meet the witness. The witness went to see a doctor, so I had very little time to talk to her, because there was a possibility that she would testify on Friday. She was ready to testify on Friday, and then it was referred until today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That may be so again, but nevertheless, have you got any other books that you're going to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not concerning the psychiatric ward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any ward. Any ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Yes. But there is a book brought by the nurse from the orthopaedic ward containing some details of the operation and their notes. This is also handwritten, and during the lunch break, I will prepare copies and give them to the Prosecution, although this witness will testify only in a few days' time, so that they can try to have it translated, because in the examination-in-chief, we will deal with this book. And that is the only other piece of evidence as far as I am aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. We will be very grateful to you if you can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, please look at the same date but number 383.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What is the name of this patient, and was this patient also admitted to another ward before coming to your ward, as you read the details in this book?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: He was admitted on the 27th of June, 1992. His name was Sreten Pavic, born in 1924 in Gorjani Uzice. He was a farmer. His number 10800, on the 3rd of July, 1992. He was transferred from the urological ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And looking at this page of your book, is this the only patient, along with Mr. Vasiljevic, who, according to this information, arrived from another ward and was admitted but not admitted to the hospital as such? If you would look at all the details on this page.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the two of them were admitted from other wards. This one was transferred from another ward and so was Mitar, on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So according to this protocol of patients and apart from the diagnosis and the discharge, you made the entries yourself. Mitar Vasiljevic was transferred to your ward on the 7th of July, 1992 from the orthopaedic ward, and he stayed until the 28th of August, 1992. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At that time, you were, as you said, the chief technician's deputy.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This ward of yours, can you describe what type of ward it was, whether patients were free to move about, whether they could receive visitors?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The ward was of the closed type. Visits to patients were permitted at certain times, on Thursdays from 2.00 to 4.00 p.m., and on Sundays from 2.00 to 4.00 p.m., but visits were conducted in the rooms. Our patients were not allowed to leave the ward, and the visits were monitored. This means that it was the duty of the nurses to see what visitors had brought with them. They were not allowed to bring anything made of glass, any sharp objects, pills, or anything else that could cause the patients to injure themselves or to injure the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say "monitored," and explain it like this, apart from checking what was brought in by visitors, was there any sort of physical checking? Was there anyone who was present during the conversation, at least at a distance, and viewing the interaction between the patients and visitors?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: We had to tour the patients and their visitors all the time. We couldn't be at the patient's side every moment, because we have 50 patients and there are two nurses on a shift. But they were still monitored. There were tours of the rooms. I'm not saying that the nurse was with the patient all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, was this peculiar to your ward because it was the psychiatric ward or was it the general practice in all the wards in Uzice?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. It was a special measure that applied only to the psychiatric ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, could the patients in your ward, of course, if they were physically able, leave the ward without your knowledge or the doctor's knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were they able to leave with your permission or the permission of the doctor?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: That was very rare with a visitor, but that was when a patient was ready to leave, when he was already better and was being prepared to go home, but not normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say "with visitors," are you saying that in such cases the patient could go outside the ward with one of his visitors? Is that how your answer is to be understood?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about individual patients. I can't remember exactly who these were. I can't give you names. But the doctor could give his approval when he thought a patient was ready to go home. And before going home, the patient would have a few weekends. He would be allowed to go home from the ward on Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and come back on Monday. It was only those patients, if they had visitors on other days, who were allowed to leave the ward with their relatives. But a doctor's approval was necessary. This was part of their therapy, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that it depended on the diagnosis and the state of each individual patient?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, please: If you had patients who were not able to move around except on crutches, for example, were the patients allowed to have the crutches with them?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you explain to us why and what would happen?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, because the other patients could take the crutches and use them to injure their fellow patients or members of the staff, and that is why the crutches were taken away. The patient could only use the crutches when the physiotherapist comes to visit him to do the exercises. So while a physiotherapist was with him, then he could. Or in the evening if the nurse received instructions to give the patient a walk, then the patient would walk with the nurse and with the crutches. But once that exercise was over, the crutches would be kept in a room that was not accessible to the patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, if a patient were to require crutches in order to be able to walk around alone or to try to go out, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: This would not be permitted. We would not allow the patient to use the crutches.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, in your ward was there a courtyard of any kind which would be isolated and closed off, where you could go without actually leaving the ward?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did have a courtyard. It was fenced. That is to say, we had a five metres' high partition and nobody could leave. But in order to go out into the courtyard, the patients would be supervised. They wouldn't be allowed out into this courtyard unsupervised, alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were the patients allowed at certain times to walk around the courtyard when they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: They were allowed at certain times to walk around the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were they supervised by you and your colleagues at such times?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were always supervised, always under somebody's control.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, taking Mitar Vasiljevic as a case in point, and we are attending his trial here and now, you read out his name and said you personally entered the name into the protocol book. I want to ask you now: Do you remember him personally as being one of the patients on your ward?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
