utterances.text: I remember him. I do recollect that he fell off a horse, and that's something that happens rarely. Usually, different patients come to us, a different type of patient. And of course, his leg was in a plaster cast. I think it was the left leg that was in a plaster cast.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, do you happen to recall some other details apart from the fact that you say that his left leg was in a plaster cast when he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was transferred to your ward? Do you remember how big the cast was? Do you remember any other specific features?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly, but I think the plaster cast was above the knee. Mitar was disturbed for a time. He was fixed, what we call fixed. Now, what time that was, I don't know, because we don't have the shift records, but I do remember him on the basis of those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, when you say that you remember that he was tied, does that refer to your ward or the ward he had been in previously?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to the psychiatric ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Madam, you say that you remember that for a time he was tied. Did I understand you to say that, that he was tied up?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you explain how this measure is applied? How do you fix the patient?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when the patient is disturbed and when there is the possibility of him injuring himself or others or the staff, that is when we apply this particular measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you can't remember how long this measure and procedure was applied; is that right, how long it was in place for?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned some record-keeping that you no longer have. Could you explain to us what kind of record-keeping it was, what records? You mentioned a notebook of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: They are reports according to the shifts, shift reports. And by law, we have to keep those reports for a period of two years, after which they are sent to the archives and those papers are destroyed after that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what type of report this is, who writes the report and how the report is recorded?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: It is in a book, and it says first, second, third shift. It is a book kept over 24 hours, and the nurses jot down their impressions and what they have to note, what happened during their shift. Of course, we enter the admission of patients, the discharge of patients, patients being transferred from one ward to another, things like that. All those things are recorded in this shift duty notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are any characteristic events, if anything characteristic happened while somebody was on duty, would they record those events in that notebook?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it wasn't only the admission of a patient that was entered, but if anything happened, if anything occurred that the nurse thought was of importance and by recording it, she would inform the person taking over the next shift?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This would be important for the next shift and, of course, for the patient under whose charge -- for the doctor under whose charge the patient was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How many shifts were there in a 24-hour period?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Three. Three shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that these are three shifts, each shift being eight hours?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The first shift is from 6.00 to 13.00 hours. The second is from 13.00 hours to 2000 hours, and the third shift is from 2000 hours to 0600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were those your working hours in 1992 as well?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you keep records of that kind today as well?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we keep records like that today, too, with the addition that we have an extra supervision notebook in which we enter patients that are to be particularly supervised, particular attention to be paid to these patients. We did not have this extra supervision notebook at that time. We just had an intensive care notebook. Now this is a novelty that we have introduced which makes our work easier. It facilitates the doctor's work, too. Let me qualify. In what we call extra supervision, we include patients, critical patients, patients who are most critical for that period of time. So in the course of hospitalisation, this -- their state might be aggravated, and then the doctor says that extra supervision is required for those patients, and then we would have the names of the patients and their conduct, what they eat, how they behave, everything that we notice regarding those patients requiring extra supervision must be entered and recorded in that special notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, when you spoke a moment ago about the fact that you mentioned -- that you remembered certain patients personally, you said that you remembered that that particular patient had been injured by falling off a horse. Can you remember whom -- who you learnt this from?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I learnt this, first of all, from my colleagues from the orthopaedic ward. We usually ask our colleagues why the patient has a plaster cast and why he has been transferred to our ward. Later on, talking to the patient himself, and this was just before he was discharged, I learnt the same thing. I talked to him, and he told me. It is usually the doctors who interview the patients, and we can't always accept what tell us. It need not be correct. But judging by what he told me, and I'm only a nurse, but I think that his state improved. He wasn't fully treated, in full health afterwards, but his condition had improved, and he told me that himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. And that was towards the end of his treatment in hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was towards the end of the hospital treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember something else, anything else that would be characteristic of him, any detail? Perhaps you happen to recall something else which might be of importance to us concerning that patient?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a long time ago. Many patients have come and gone, so I can't -- I don't think I can remember anything more specific at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I understand that fully. Can you explain, given the times, what the procedure for admission into hospital was, generally speaking, when a patient is brought to the hospital by an ambulance or some other way as an urgent case? What would the admission procedure be, where was the patient admitted, where was he recorded and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: All the admissions are recorded in the admission book and the staff has the protocol for the entire hospital, protocol book for the entire hospital, and you can see where each patient is -- which wards the patients are in. I know that people come in very often. One of the people they know have been admitted into hospital, and they don't know which ward to find them in. And then my colleague will look at the protocol book, go through the names and the numbers, and would find the patient's name and be able to tell which ward the patient was in. And I think at that time, in the afternoon and at night, the case history and recording of the patient is done at the admissions department in the emergency service, and this would be entered into the protocol book of that admissions emergency service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, you said that reading through the data, and look at 386 again, please, number 386, in the one but last column, that 1014 is the number of the case history for the patient Mitar Vasiljevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That particular number, is it the number which relates to the whole of the general hospital regardless of the ward, and is that the only number that a patient can have?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the only number that this patient can have. Each patient, when admitted to hospital, gets his own personal number, and you can see from the later columns that the numbers are different. The numbers differ. And until he is released, discharged to go home and a discharge letter written, he has this one particular number, the number of his case history. It goes with him all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So is that number assigned to the patient once he entered the hospital, as soon as he entered the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the number assigned upon admission into hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that in this particular case, the case of Mitar Vasiljevic, the next person who is admitted and recorded would be 10015?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next patient admitted into hospital after him would get the next number, 10015, and the one after that would be 10016, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, that would apply regardless of the ward the patient is assigned to. So in the case of Mitar Vasiljevic, he was sent to the orthopaedic ward; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, regardless of what ward he's sent to, regardless. A patient cannot be admitted to two wards. He can't have two case histories. He can be admitted to one ward with one case history, and then he can be transferred from one ward to another, from the psychiatric ward to another ward, but he carries all his documents with him. He has one case history, the one he received upon admission into hospital, when he entered hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. But just to make things quite clear, he was admitted to the orthopaedic ward and got the number that was free, the next free number, which was 10014. Now, if the next patient, for example, was admitted to the urological ward, would he be 10015? Would that number be assigned, the next number in order? Is that what I understand you to say?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the very next number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you say, Mrs. Tomasevic, that the case history follows the patient and that that is the same number when he is transferred from one ward to another? Does that mean that all the documents which were in the previous ward follows the patient; his dossier and case history moves with him to the next ward where he is transferred?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. All the documentation moves with the patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In this particular case, would that mean that when Mitar Vasiljevic was transferred to your ward, that his whole file, his dossier, his case history which was number 10014 was transferred to your ward? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If in a file dossier of that kind there was any X-rays from the previous ward, would those X-rays, by regular procedure, be attached to the file, to the whole file?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a rule, they would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When the patient leaves your ward and the case history is closed, completed, where are the documents stored, the case history plus all the other documents within the file, that patient's file? Where would they be stored?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The case history goes to the archives where it remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say "archives," Mrs. Tomasevic, there is an archive for the entire hospital or does each ward have its own archive?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: It is an archive for all the wards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood you. Are you saying that the archive for all the wards is in one place, that there is one archive for the hospital, or are there several?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the kind of -- there are several archives, but you have the hospital archive but at different locations. It's not distributed for the department, the wards, but perhaps -- there are a lot of case histories. So I'm not sure if they're all stored in one place, one room, because there might be too many of them. That I don't know, but it's one archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. What you're saying is you don't know how many rooms the archive comprises, but if I understand you correctly, as an organisational unit, there is just one archive for the general hospital at Uzice. Is that what you're saying? Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you have understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you spoke about your ward, which is a ward with beds, I think you mentioned this, but could you tell me how many rooms and how many beds did your ward consist of at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Fifty beds. And the surface area, well, it's not a large surface area. I cannot tell you the surface area, but I do know that we had 50 beds, not many staff, two technicians per shift, in fact, two nurses or two technicians per shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I wasn't thinking about surface area. I was thinking of rooms. How many rooms and how many beds to a room and so on.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I see, rooms. Well, let me see. One, two -- seven rooms. One room had 16 beds, one had 14 beds, and the rest I can't be sure. We had two rooms with four beds, six beds, depending on the room. It was an old ward, but roughly that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, from these records or from any other records, would you able to see which doctor was in charge of which patient? And in this case, Mitar Vasiljevic, who was he assigned to?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: From these records, as they were kept at the time, this can't be seen. But later on -- you wouldn't see that from these entries. But later on, in addition, we would enter the doctor's name. So in later reports, one could see which doctor attended which patient. But from the protocol later on, you would be able to see the name of the doctor who treated the patient, but not at this particular period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say "later on," I don't understand when you mean. Do you mean that in later periods this was recorded and not at that period of time or -- I'm not sure I understood what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: When our head -- the head of the service and the main nurse or principal technician was changed, I and the head nurse and the head of the department agreed that in addition to these columns that existed, we should add a column with the name of the doctor supervising the patient, for many reasons, of course. First, that we would know if -- when a family member came, which doctor they could contact or which doctor we could contact for a particular case history, and for many other reasons, of course. So this was introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But if I understood you correctly, in this period, and I'm referring to July 1992, records of this kind were not kept in this book.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you cannot answer my question as to which doctor, according to this book, was in charge?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I can't tell you that from just looking at this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you tell me if, apart from the hospital treatment you provided, you also catered for outpatients.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was the outpatient clinic physically separate from the ward you were talking about where the inpatients were? I'm referring to the location of the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: It was in a separate location, and a separate protocol was kept. It was again a protocol of patients, but other details were entered. And this was separate. It was not in the same building. It had nothing to do with the ward. There were other nurses or, rather, one nurse working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When the patients who had formerly been treated in your ward came for check-ups, were the check-ups carried out in your ward or in the outpatients clinic you have just described?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Check-ups were conducted in the outpatients clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The doctors in the outpatients clinic, were they the same doctors working in the ward or were they completely different doctors in the outpatients ward and the inpatients ward?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: It was the doctors from the ward who worked in the outpatients clinic. They had days when they worked in the outpatients clinic so that on each day there was a doctor assigned to the outpatients clinic, and on that day he would conduct his rounds of the ward and then go to the outpatients clinic to work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you personally know whether on his discharge from hospital Mitar Vasiljevic regularly came for check-ups in the outpatients clinic of your hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I personally am not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Why? Was it the reason you have just described?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It's not that I don't have access, but I'm not there. I don't go there. I wasn't working there. And you know, we have thousands of patients passing through the outpatients clinic per year. So had I been working there, I would not be able to remember. I think there are at least 6.000 patients a year who pass through that outpatients clinic. So it's very difficult. It can only be seen from a book like this one. Of course, in the outpatients clinic, it was other details that were entered, the first and last name, of course, but sick leave days and the diagnosis and the number of the medical booklet, the number of the insurance and the type of insurance. So other details then were entered in this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So the outpatients clinic of your ward has quite separate records for its patients; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you tell me, please, if you remember if your ward admitted such patients, was the war theatre or battlefield used as a place from which they arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What did this term, as far as you know, mean, the term "war front," when it was entered?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: It referred to the area where military operations were being conducted or, rather, the area affected by war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to go back for a moment to the procedure you described. When you said that the doctors working in the ward had certain Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. days on which they were assigned to the outpatients clinic, did this also refer to the nurses or were the nurses assigned only to the ward or to the outpatients clinic?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: It was always one nurse working in the outpatients clinic and possibly another one standing in for her when she was on annual leave. But the sisters -- the nurses in the outpatients clinic did not change except if she went on sick leave or annual leave, in which case there would be another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. So in principle, there was one group of nurses assigned to the ward and another group of nurses assigned to the outpatients clinic.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct. One for the ward and one for the outpatients clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And finally, to go back to the book you are holding in front of you, before you, this is the book only of those who were actually in bed, who were hospitalised?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are only patients in the psychiatric ward. There was another book for the outpatients clinic, which has nothing to do with this one. So the outpatients clinic and the ward and the records kept for the former and the latter had nothing in common except for superficial similarities. But they were kept differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. And to conclude, let me ask you, Mrs. Tomasevic, you know that today you are a witness under oath. Do you still say that the details entered in this original book relating to Mitar Vasiljevic and the others on this page, that you, yourself, made the entries you have explained to us today, and that this was done in 1992, as you said?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am under oath, and before God and before this Court, I say that what I said today is how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one more question. When a patient is leaving the hospital, is it sometimes the spouse of the patient who asks for a patient to be released before the doctors feel that he or she is ready, and what is done in such situations?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it does happen. We do not have the right to keep someone in the ward by force unless we have a court order. In any other case, close relatives can come, people who live with the patient, and they can ask for their child or husband or wife to be released, and it would be against the law not to do it, because if there is no court order and treatment has not been ordered by a court, then the relatives do have the right to take the patient home. Of course, they have to sign, because if they are taking the patient home at their request and the doctor feels the patient has not been cured, it is the relatives who are taking the responsibility and the risk on themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I understand. So in that case, the close family member has to sign personally that he or she is taking the patient home at his or her own request.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is done by the doctor in charge, the doctor in charge of the patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What do you want done with the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, I know that this is the original book you have brought with you. I think it would be important for the original to stay here for a while, while these proceedings are in progress. Would it be possible for you to leave this book with us?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: It is possible, but who guarantees that I will get it back because --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, it should stay here for a time. So could you explain that to your hospital? You can get a receipt for the book. Because I would like IT to be kept here for the time being as an exhibit in this case.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I just hope that in a certain time I will get it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I wish to tender this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, you were able, in relation to the other books, to provide copies, were you not, for the hospital to use in case they needed them in the meantime? I don't know whether you did it for all three books. It seemed to have got into evidence, but certainly one of them did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you know that the -- one of the protocols we have managed to photocopy. It took two evenings to do it, two days. On Saturday, I tried to copy this book. It's very difficult, because the format is larger than usual. If necessary, perhaps a photocopy could be made later on for their use, but I think the original should stay here in any case, and I don't think that this will cause major problems for the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's a matter for you, Mr. Domazet. I should think that whilst it might take a week or so, someone in the registry could be put to the task. We seem to have so many people down there. Somebody would be able to do it for us. But I agree with you, if the book is going to be tendered, it should be the original. What is your attitude, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not had an opportunity to examine this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm asking whether you object to its admissibility. You don't have to examine it for that reason. Is there any reason why it should not be admitted in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Having not seen the book, Your Honour, I have no objection I can make to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What is the next number? 29, is it Mr. Domazet? That's my next number, but have you already assigned it to any other document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. It will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It can be 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Exhibit 29. Now, 26 is one where we have a copy of it. Twenty-seven, we have a copy of part of it, as I recall, and 28 we have no copies of. I'll give a direction that photostat copies be made of those books with respect to the relevant hospital or medical centres so that the originals can stay here until the matter is disposed off. Yes, Mr. Groome. Are you cross-examining?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Tomasevic. My name is Dermot Groome, and I will be asking you questions on behalf of the Prosecution in this case. Can I ask you a few questions about the medical or the records that you ever here? You've told us that all of the writing in this book is in Cyrillic, and my question to you is: Are all medical records -- is there a rule about keeping medical records in Cyrillic? Is that a hospital rule?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: There are no rules. You can write either in Latin or Cyrillic script. There is no rule as to what script we should use.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it just happens that all of the writing in this particular book is in Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Mostly, yes. It depends on us, the staff, how we write. I myself write in the Cyrillic script. But when I write capital letters, I write in the Latin script. So I don't like to use -- when it's longhand, then I write Cyrillic, in the Cyrillic script. When it's capital letters for the Latin alphabet -- I use capital letters for the Latin script. I can show you if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, no. I believe you. My next question for you is: Where do you record information regarding what medications are given to patients on the psychiatric ward?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: That is written on a therapy list, and the nurses keep the therapy lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, let me see. I think you've mentioned three different records pertaining to the patients on the psychiatric ward. This protocol and the document you referred to as the shift report, and this third document that you're telling us about now, the therapy list. Are those all -- those three different records, do they all pertain to patients on the psychiatric ward?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Aside from those three, are there any other records that you maintain on your ward?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you, we have the extra supervision notebook, the book of therapy as regards time per hour, muscular therapy usually, so all those documents. But that was in 1992. So looking back to 1992, all that remains is this. Now, we have made an innovation in psychiatry, and that is the extra supervision notebook, listing the patients that need special attention, special supervision. But for us, it is important to note that they are in a serious psychological state and that we have to exert extra supervision. I'm not saying that we don't supervise and pay attention to other patients, but these are under special, extra supervision. They are not allowed out into the courtroom [as interpreted], that is one specification. Visits to these patients are limited. The doctor determines who can visit the patient. And it is also happens that patients don't want to receive visits. They might quarrel with their visitors. There are different incidents that can crop up with respect to visitors. So it is difficult to work with psychiatric patients generally. I don't know how far you can understand this, how you can understand me, but our patients are, unfortunately, difficult patients, and we have no way in which to prevent them from escaping. We have to have iron bars as well on our wards to prevent patients from jumping out of the window, for example, because our building is a two-storey building. So this is an extra feature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Groome. I don't blame you for stopping that. This is not an answer to your question. But there was a reference there to being let out into the courtyard. It's now been corrected, I see. It's courtyard, yes. The translation said "courtroom" but it's been corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's okay. But anyway, you can take her back to your question, are there any other records.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the therapy list that you're talking about. Is there a different one for every patient or is there a different one for all the patients on the ward at a particular time?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: When we have therapy lists, we have -- they are uniform for all those patients. We have a shortage of medicines sometimes. We have a shortage of resources, so sometimes we write it down on the temperature list. There's a temperature list that includes blood pressure and so on. We have to put them in a file this big, and this prevents the patient from knowing what they're being given, because patients are not allowed to know what therapy they're being given. If it's written up on their bed, then they come to us and say, "Why am I taking this particular therapy? I don't want to take that therapy." So it's because of the patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, would I be correct in thinking that there is a list of medicines that Mr. Vasiljevic received as part of his case history file? Is there -- there should be a file listing the medications that he received during his time on the psychiatric ward?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: In the documentation, that list ought to exist, yes. When we complete the case history, the case history file should including the therapy list. Now, what format it was, I can't tell you. It was a long time ago. What format the list was. I can tell you what formats are used now, the formats, but very often we don't have the necessary formats and printed forms, so we have to improvise. And yes, our patients are not allowed to see what therapy they are getting, what particular medicaments, unless the doctor decides to tell them, but they cannot read this for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, I am going to hand you a blank piece of paper. I'm going to ask that it be noted as Prosecution document 159. I'm going to ask you if you would -- I'm not sure if there is a pen up there. If you would just take a pen and would you just copy out Mr. Vasiljevic's entry. Just copy it out for us. Yes, write on the desk and not on the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is the list, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, just the entry she made regarding Mr. Vasiljevic on the day he was admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's not the document we've already got?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want everything from start to finish, from beginning to end?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just for Mr. Vasiljevic. You talked about several entries, several notes that you made regarding Mr. Vasiljevic, his name, his date of birth. Just that single line, if you would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And just to get it clear there, this is from the case history file, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's from D29 and its ordinal number 386.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Miss, I would ask you not to write on the book itself, Miss Tomasevic. I would ask if the witness could be directed just to write on the desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I am still not clear. Are you asking her to copy out what is written in this document that is Exhibit 29?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just my handwriting or everything?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just your handwriting. The note that you wrote back when you admitted Mr. Vasiljevic. If you could just copy that entry out for us. I'm sorry, Miss. Did you write this for us or is it the Cyrillic alphabet?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Cyrillic. Cyrillic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would tender that as Prosecution Exhibit 159.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Show the document to Mr. Domazet. Any objection, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not have an objection, but if I understand that this is for some purpose of comparison, I know that in this kind of situation, it is necessary for her to write it ten times. That is as far as I know for that kind of expertise. So she ought to write it ten times, at least if Mr. Groome is to use it for comparison purposes. I don't think that this is sufficient data and that this might give rise to problems. So to avoid those, I suggest that, but I have nothing against having this admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't always repeat it in exactly the same way, but you can compare the two and you can see that it is my handwriting. Of course, I can never write it identically unless I were to place a piece of indigo carbon underneath but it is certainly my writing. Now, sometimes I can write nice -- more beautifully. If I'm writing slower, I'll form the letters better but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I would not agree with Mr. Domazet that it has to be ten times unless there is some special law in the former Yugoslavia which says so, but it is usual to have more than one if this is for the purpose of handwriting comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I could ask as we take the break if the witness could remain for five minutes and perhaps write the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I would have thought three times would have been sufficient, but I'm in your hands. I've never seen it done more --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can write it as many times as you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Madam, please, just let us work this one out. We'll work it out with you in a moment. In 40 something years' experience I've never seen it done more these times, but how many times do you suggest that she should do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: From what I know of these tests, I thought the one was sufficient. Three times would be a very happy compromise for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, madam, we'd like you to write it out another two times, if you would, on the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I would just ask that the witness not write on the ledger book as that could also affect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I agree with you entirely. Somebody will have to stay with the witness while she does it, but I don't think we need to. We'll adjourn now until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 22 23 24 25 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few more questions about how the hospital keeps records, and the first question I'd like to ask you is the hospital archive, where is that located precisely?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: In the hospital building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Have you ever, yourself, actually been into the archive?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where in the hospital is it located? Is it a basement storage area? Is it a separate building?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: In the basement. Well, they're in several locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe, is it -- are the archives spread out among the years or is it departments? How do they decide which of these several locations documents are going to be archived?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: I can't actually tell you, because that's not something that I would know, although I do know that the archive has a protocol book of its own. It is the hospital archive, and I think that it has numbers or the alphabet, goes by the alphabet, "T," "M," on the basis of the surnames of the patients, that it is ordered in that way, in alphabetical order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, maybe you can explain in this case, you've brought one of the books from the archive. Can you explain to us the procedure that you have to follow in order to get possession of that book?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: This particular protocol book is one that I keep under lock and key. It is under the lock and key of the head nurse. It's not the protocol that I took from the archive. The case history goes to the archive, but the protocol book stays in the ward so that we are able to get information. People might come to ask about patients, whether they were treated or not, how they were treated, and then I refer back to the protocol book. They tell us the year in which the patient -- approximately the year the patient was in the hospital. They're not always sure whether it was 1992 or 1993. And in that protocol, we can look for that person, to see whether the patient was hospitalised or not, and then that is taken to the archive. And at a court request -- upon a court order, the court can request the protocol and information from it. I don't actually know what the procedure is after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I believe you told us in your direct testimony that this book, particular protocol book that you brought with you, was in use up until June of 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to us, on a daily basis, where is the book kept so that the head nurse can make entries into the book? Is it kept on her desk or his desk?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: You mean during those years. Well, until the protocol book is filled up, it is in the outpatients department and accessible to the nurses to see whether the patient is there for other things, that they can write him in, a patient in, if we're not there, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the book that you brought to us in court, after it was finished was placed in the outpatient department? Did I hear you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. When the protocol book is filled out, I keep it under lock and key. When it's complete, then it's locked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question to you is: When you're using it. So the period of 1991, I believe this book began, and it was completed in June of 1994. During all those three years, where was the book kept on a daily basis? Was is on the desk of the head nurse?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. It was in the working premises, the working room, that is to say, the staff employed in the psychiatric ward, the nurses, would have access to it. It was in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us, who can make notes in this book? I believe you're telling us now that nurses can make notes in this book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly this is done by the head nurse. If it is done by some of the other staff during a shift so that we don't forget to write someone in, then it is the head nurse or head technician, depending on who's on duty, must check through it, because each patient must be inscribed. And if there is a case history, the case history is taken on the rounds, the doctor's rounds. But some of the doctors might go off duty, so we carry the case history around while we make our tour, our visit of the patient. We can read what there is in the case history, and if there is a deterioration in the patient's state, the therapy might have to be corrected. So even the people -- the physician whose patient it is -- even if it is not the patient in -- the doctor in charge of the patient who is present, we can pass the information on to the person who is on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So nurses can make entries into it and doctors can make entries into this book; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are there any other staff on the psychiatric ward, either orderlies or assistants, who make entries into the book if they need to?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned something about the psychiatric ward being very different than the other wards in that it was a closed ward. Can I take that -- from that that the patients in the other wards, the open wards, that it is possible for them to leave and return if they so wish to do?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: As to how things functioned in other wards, I can't actually say, but in principle, no patient can leave a ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us what is the procedure for somebody on your ward if they want to leave? Let's say a family member comes and they went to go for a walk with that family member. What procedure is followed before that person can be allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: He must have permission from the doctor for him to go outside the compound of the ward. I said that he -- they can go into the courtyard but it is controlled, supervised, so that is closed, too. But it happens that patients spend two or three weekends at home. They are trial weekends, so to speak, to see how the patient is going to accept home treatment, whether they can find their way in the home environment. And after spending two or three weekends at home or how much as the doctor allows the patient, then he gives the permission ultimately but he has to tell us. And he says to us, "Yes, you can let that patient go out and have a walk with his relatives for such and such a time but he must come back." So you know the exact time when he can leave, by which time he has to be back and how much time he can spend.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us where in the record is it recorded that a person has left on one of these weekend visits that you're describing for us?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: There is the weekend book, a book for weekends, and it says "Left then," and "Is allowed out from then to then," and so on. Or if we allow somebody to leave for an afternoon, that is also recorded in the shift book. But if patients go off on a weekend, they must have a permit from the doctor which says -- states the name and surname of the patient, his personal identification number, the time he is allowed to leave for and the therapy he must take. So if he goes out for a day during the weekend and has had his morning therapy in the hospital, he has to have his therapy -- afternoon therapy at home as we specify, which medicines are to be taken and so on. But they must always be accompanied. A patient always has a person to accompany him. They never go alone, always with a close member of his family, that is to say, a member of the household. He cannot accompanied by a distant relation. A distant relative cannot take a patient out of a hospital or take them home for the weekend or anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I thought before the break we had identified three records. It appears now there is a fourth record. I'm sorry, I want to ask you again: Are the four records that pertain to a patient in the psychiatric ward the protocol, the shift book, the therapy list and the weekend book; are those the fourth book?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: There's the weekend book, too, and the intensive care book.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But the intensive care book I believe you told us did not come into play until after 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. The intensive care book did exist in 1992 but the intensive care book is something else. Those are people with organic disturbances, deliriums which are life threatening, where we have to monitor three times a day their blood pressure, temperature, the uresis [phoen], and the general state of the patient is such that it requires intensive care. So if there are any changes for the worse, we must consult the consultants. He is not only suffering from psychological disorders, he also has an organic disorder as well. So that is the intensive care book or notebook, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, of these five books, did you bring any of these other books other than the protocol? Did you bring any of these other books with you with respect to Mr. Vasiljevic in June and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would I be correct in thinking from your description or concluding from your description of the shift book that the shift book would actually have more information about the daily activities and more information about the daily life of Mr. Vasiljevic in the psychiatric ward during this time period?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: It's like this: At the beginning when his state was poor, he was mentioned in the shift notebooks, and it would be interesting if I had that, but we don't have it because by law we store those books for a period of two years. After that, we're not obliged by law to keep them, because we would have too much paperwork. And there was also the transfer of service, and from one building to another. So probably it is possible that it was handed over to this other service and that that is why those documents do not exist. So we can't keep records of all 50 patients, just the ones that are disturbed or fixed or threaten to commit suicide or something specific, some specific state which we consider merits being recorded for the doctors to be able to read this when they come in, in the morning. They read these reports in the morning or when they're on duty. So they have to read the reports for the previous day when they come on duty, and they must talk to the patient on the basis of what they have read, and then they are able to see on the basis of that conversation whether this is our own impression that is not perhaps vital. They -- we are nurses and they are doctors, so we can't always know what is important. Sometimes things that we as nurses consider important, doctors do not see to be relevant, that these symptoms are normal for that patient suffering from that kind of illness. So it is the doctor that differentiates and distinguishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you now. You describe Mr. Vasiljevic as having been a fixed patient, which I believe means he was tied up. It doesn't seem as if there's any record of that in the protocol book.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There is no record of that no the protocol book; corrects?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. That is in written in the records and we don't have the reports. Those kinds of things are written in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So when you testified earlier about remembering that, that was your own independent memory. It wasn't something that you refreshed your memory before to coming to court here with some other documents? Is that what your testimony is?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. I have nowhere to read it in any document. I didn't read it anywhere. I told you what I said was that he was fixed for a time, tied up for a time. I can't tell you how long for, but I said that I remember because he -- I learnt that he had fallen from a horse. That's something that I remembered and then I remembered him being tied. So -- and I learnt this talking to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: So that's what stuck in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you this about being tied: Is your memory that he came to the ward tied or was the decision made to tie him up after he was observed on the ward for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: When I came to The Hague, started out for The Hague, I had to talk to my colleague who worked on -- who was in the shift then, and she remembers. I found Mitar tied the next day, but she remembers admitting him and that he was tied during admission, when admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you told us that a person is tied if they are a threat to themselves or to others, and my question to you is: In this particular case of Mr. Vasiljevic, do you know or do you recall whether he was tied because he was a threat to himself or was he a threat to other patients and staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember that. He was disturbed, unsettled, and he could have broken the plaster cast he had. Now, whether he could injure anybody else, I don't know but it was a measure of -- a safety measure because he was agitated. So if he was agitated, he could have removed the work of what -- of the doctors previously who had placed the plaster cast on his leg. He might have tried to take it off. Now, the question -- I don't know whether he was a danger to anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you some specific questions about your observations of Mr. Vasiljevic, but before that, I just have a few questions more on the records. Now, when you filled out the protocol book, am I correct in thinking that the date of the 14th of June, that was a date that you copied over from the case history report? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you, yourself, have no personal knowledge of when Mr. Vasiljevic actually entered Uzice hospital, you simply transferred the information that you found on one hospital document to your ledger or your protocol ledger; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's right. What was entered into the protocol was transferred from the case history. So I don't know when he was admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, another question about the shift report. I believe you told us in response to a question by Mr. Domazet that the admission of a patient is also noted on the shift report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I wonder if you'd give us the benefit of your over 20 years of experience on the psychiatric ward. I'm going to ask you: Have you been involved in the treatment of alcoholics on that ward before?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Alcoholics are treated in the stage of an alcoholic psychosis or delirium. So they stay for a very short period of time, usually seven days. Sometimes we would place three psychiatric patients into one bed. Those were the circumstances. We were completely overbooked at that time. So yes, I did work with delirious patients. That is correct. But their stay in our institution would only be for them to recover, organically speaking, until they would quieten down, and then they would go home. Then they would go to the alcoholics institute for further treatment. We are an institution for acute disorders. So once we had dealt with that stage, we would discharge the patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you say that an alcoholic would be treated for a short period of time and you gave us the number of seven days. Am I correct in saying that would be the period of time that the person would be in withdrawal, their body would experience the effects of not having alcohol every day? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I am not an expert, but with abstinence, abstinence brings about delirium tremens. Now the cause is of etherism, and I can tell you that from my own experience, but you cannot take that for court purposes because I'm not an expert in that area, but there are symptomatic, what we call symptomatic alcoholism. So people suffering from -- alcoholism is a mask for other disorders and disturbances, and when I flew in a plane for the first time I had a drink, for example, to relax, to cover my fear of flying, and so individual patients do the same thing. By drinking, they are in fact masking some other fear. But a doctor can tell you that. I can only tell you as far as my professional training allows me as a nurse, but that is not a valid professional opinion in the sense of a doctor giving it. So I don't -- I can't talk about something that is not in my domain of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What I'm trying to get at is that in your experience, this seven-day period you've mentioned, that would be the period of time that somebody who is abstaining from alcohol, that is the period of time it takes their body to adjust to no longer having alcohol; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: He recovers in the course of these seven days, seven to ten days. He recovers because he doesn't drink. He is given liquid. He is under certain therapy. Now, whether he has been treated completely, no, because alcoholism is a long process.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Correct. Now, --

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Whether he hasn't been cured.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you assist me in this question then? After a person who is an alcoholic, let's assume a severe alcoholic, after they cease to drink, what period of time -- how long does it take for the -- this delirium to set in? What is the person between the time the person stops taking alcohol and then begins to show the effects of not taking alcohol? Is it a day, two days, three days?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you an answer to that question. It is not under my domain of expertise. I'm not trained sufficiently, qualified to give you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during this time period in your work on the ward, on the psychiatric ward, would it be fair to say that a number of the patients were there because they were overwhelmed by some of the horrible things that they had witnessed in this conflict, that that was the root cause of their psychiatric problem?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. A large number of patients were there for -- the number of patients increased. And I looked at -- did some statistical data and report for my graduate thesis and I saw that the numbers had increased. And it wasn't easy for us, the staff there either. And it was a period when we had a shortage of medicines and so when a patient would come, you wouldn't have the necessary sedatives. It was a very -- extremely difficult period for us, the hospital staff, and for the patients as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, would it also be fair to say that out of that group of increased patients, that at least some of them, the precipitating event was guilt over their participation in some of the horrible things that they had witnessed? It was a sense of guilt that troubled them so. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So for all these patients that you've been involved in their treatment, not one ever expressed a sentiment of feeling guilty for some of the things that happened?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. Those are questions which we cannot ask our patients, and we cannot -- because you know how it is. We can provoke a patient by asking -- I can't come by that information. I can't ask that. They must be highly controlled conversations. You must have controlled conversations with psychiatric patients. We can't talk to them much. We can only ask them general things. But we cannot enter into the domain of the cause of their diseases. We are not allowed do that. We can aggravate the patient's state. They can see somebody else in us. They can see somebody who is threatening them, jeopardising them in some way. For example, once I asked a female patient for a book. I thought she was in remission. That was my assessment of her, that she was getting better. But the next day she complained to the doctor and said that I was controlling her, that I had something against her and was exerting control over her just asking her for a book. She was a teacher and I needed the book and I just happened to ask her for the book, and I thought she was feeling much better. She was in remission, and that's why I asked her for the book. So we're not allowed to engage in conversations and details of that kind with the patients. Nurses are not allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the drug Trodon, T-R-O-D-O-N?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is that sedative that is used psychiatric patients to calm them down?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Trodon is a medicine against pain, as far as I know, a pain-killer. In the case of very strong pain, Trodon is administered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it ever administered as a sedative to patients?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, on the entry that you made for Mr. Vasiljevic, under the column that I believe is for diagnosis, you wrote "298.9." My question to you is, what does 298.9 refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't write that down. That is not my handwriting. And it means that the discharge diagnosis of the patient when he left to go home. You can compare it. You will see it is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if you could help me to understand. On the protocol book, what columns did you not write? I was under the impression that you had written those numbers.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. Where the diagnosis is, I didn't fill in. All the other columns I did, but the diagnosis, that's not mine. The main technician came home from leave. He looked at the case history, and he made that entry. That is not my handwriting. And that can very easily be compared. If you have any documents from us, you will see whether that is in order or not. But I am sure it must correspond. If you have the case history or anything, the first page of the case history must correspond to those numbers, the registration number and all these other numbers, and the code numbers, they have to correspond. You told me there were two codes there, didn't you, two numbers? And I saw two, but that is not my handwriting. I didn't write that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting of the person who made that assessment and note in the record?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I am not sure, but I think it was the main technician who came home from leave and that he made that entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know that person's name?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: His name is Nikola. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And his family name?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Jaksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The other entry is 823.2, and there is a question mark after it. Based on your experience, what would that question mark mean for you?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Probably somebody was surprised by the diagnosis, because according to our system of codes, it doesn't fit because it's not a psychiatric code. It's an orthopaedic code. I am not aware that there was any such diagnostic code in psychiatry, even according to the old system. But if a patient has several diagnoses, then all five have to be entered. He may not just be a psychiatric patient. He may also be an internal medical case, a neurological case, but he was treated at the psychiatric ward but under the occasional control of other doctors. And when he goes home, in addition to his psychiatric diagnosis, all the other illnesses that he suffers from are also diagnosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, even though you yourself did not make these notes, can you help us by telling us what does 298.9 stand for? What is that a diagnosis of?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I am not qualified for that, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, surely 20 years working with these protocols, surely, you must know when you see that what type of patient we are dealing with; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that. I'm not allowed to interfere with diagnosis. I must not say what the diagnosis is because I'm not qualified for that. I would need far more schooling to be qualified to be able to tell you what diagnosis that is. Very generally speaking, I think it is psychosis, but psychosis is a very wide term. Now you're going to ask me what kind of psychosis and things like that. These are things I am unable to answer. They studied for ten years to become psychiatrists.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mrs. Tomasevic, a patient who is on the ward because they are an alcoholic, would this code be used or is there a separate, special code for somebody who is on the ward for being alcoholic?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? Which number?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The 298.9. Would that code be used in the case of somebody who is an alcoholic and is on the ward for treatment or is there a different number that refers to an alcoholic -- a person who is going through -- delirium because of alcoholism?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. There are various classifications of delirium and alcoholism and psychosis, so I'm really not able to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not asking you for a diagnosis, but simply in your experience, your 20 years of experience, what code would ordinarily be used for somebody who is an alcoholic on your ward? Is it this one or is it a different number?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The code, you see, these are old codes, let me point out. That was in 1992. So I can't tell you exactly what those codes meant then. Can't you understand me? I'm not sure whether it's delirium tremens according to the new classification. And what it was then, I don't know. My superiors would tell me, "How were you able to say that when you are not qualified?" I may be held responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Looking over the one page that I've been given, it looks like approximately a third to a half of the diagnosis boxes are left blank. What would that indicate, that a diagnosis block has been left blank?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that question either. I wasn't doing that work then. I entered the patient -- I recorded the patients when they were admitted. Now what happened after that, I'm unable to say. Maybe the documents went to the archives without the number being entered. But in any event, what is registered there is what it is. In my opinion, that is exactly how it was. That was not my job at the time. My job ended once I entered the name of the patient. Then my colleague came from his leave in 1992, already in October. I went to Belgrade to attend a higher nursing school, so I don't know what happened. When the offices were moved, I wasn't there. Why these entries were not filled in, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let me ask you based on your responsibilities now as the head nurse of the psychiatric ward. Would you be surprised at seeing blank entries for diagnosis now and would you attempt to speak with the doctor or somebody to have that corrected? Would you see that as an irregularity now as head nurse?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: When a patient is being discharged, that is, when the patient is admitted, we don't write down the diagnosis because it is what we call a working diagnosis. The final diagnosis is the one with which the patient is sent home, and it is written on the case history. It says "Final diagnosis." There's a column there, and it has to be entered. That final diagnosis has to be in that column. It can't be the initial diagnosis, because a patient is under observation. What happens sometimes is that a patient is sent to the hospital under one diagnosis, and after observation and discussions with the doctors and examinations, he's given a different diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you about one other number on the protocol, and that's the one -- 10014 number, and you told us that was the patient identification number; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the patient identification number, as we call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you the following question to see if I understand how this number works: If I am admitted to the hospital in Uzice and I remain there for a month, I will be assigned a number. If I leave the hospital and after two days of being at home I need to be readmitted to the hospital, do I get a new number or do I still use my old patient identification number?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No, you get a new number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you told us that -- I'm sorry. Withdraw that. Do you recall whether of your observations of Mr. Vasiljevic whether in your opinion, based on your experience, he was going through the symptoms of somebody withdrawing from alcohol?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the 7th of July was a holiday. You were off, and when you came in to work on the 8th of July, Mr. Vasiljevic was already on the ward; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that a routine transfer on such a holiday -- I'm sorry, that routine transfers would ordinarily occur on working days, that there must have been something special or some type of emergency that required Mr. Vasiljevic to be transferred to the psychiatric ward on the 7th, on a holiday? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise. The fact that he was transferred on the 7th, a holiday, would that indicate to you that there was some type of emergency or some type of precipitating event that required his transfer on the 7th rather than simply wait until the 8th, on an ordinary business day, for a transfer?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That must have been an emergency as soon as he was transferred during a holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you recall what that was?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, do I remember? I'm afraid I don't understand what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall what the emergency was that required Mr. Vasiljevic to be transferred on the 7th rather than waiting until the 8th?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't working on the 7th, but my colleague who admitted him said that he was agitated, that he was shouting, cursing. The very fact that he had to be tied up means that he was disturbing other patients in the orthopaedics ward. He could have hurt himself, you see. It's on the third or fourth floor - I don't recall any longer - and they're afraid of psychiatric patients, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to show you the case history for Mr. Vasiljevic, and it's Exhibit P138. I'm going to draw your attention to the note made on the 7th of July. The English translation of this is Prosecution Exhibit number 62, and I have some extra copies if the Court would prefer, if it's more convenient for me to hand up these copies. Is it? Can you find the note for the 7th of July by Dr. Stojkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. What it says for the 7th of July, Dr. Stojkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Already several pages there. Perhaps it may be on one of the other pages that you're not looking at at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, isn't it a fact that the precipitating event, the emergency that required his transfer to the psychiatric ward was that he physically attacked a Muslim patient? Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have a copy?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: It depends on his medical condition, because you see, the signature here is of the psychiatrist, to be moved to the ward, Dr. Bogdanovic, that is his signature. I know him. He died. He believed that because of his mental condition, this had occurred. If it had been anything else, he wouldn't have been transferred to our ward. As far as I can see here, the discharge document, he hasn't had it certified. There are two more pieces of paper in the case history. There should be two more pieces of paper. One is the bill and report on hospitalisation, and those two additional pieces of paper have to be identical. And until all that is done, he is still a patient of the hospital. He was a hospital patient because his discharge paper was not certified, and until that is done, he continues to be the patient of the hospital. The fact that he was given the discharge document doesn't mean that he left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't think that's an answer to the question, but why do you let it go for so long? You asked whether or not a particular event caused his transfer to the psychiatric ward. Now, nothing that the witness has said has answered that question that I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I just -- I do try and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We really do have to move on and stop these long, unresponsive answers. If you want the question answered, ask it again. And madam, please just answer the question. If you are then asked for an explanation, you may give the explanation, but please just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you answer -- please answer my question yes or no and I'll ask for additional information if I need it. Looking at the note on the 7th of July, is it not a fact that the precipitating emergency was that Mr. Vasiljevic had physically attacked a Muslim patient? Isn't that correct? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you see the portion of the medical record, the case history on the note from the 7th of July? Are you looking at that portion of the medical history?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you see a note there saying that Mr. Vasiljevic attacked a Muslim patient?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you also see a note there that Mr. Vasiljevic was lingering in the main hall of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would a physical attack by one patient on another patient, would that be the type of event that would require somebody's immediate transfer to the psychiatric ward on a holiday such as the 7th? Is that the kind of thing that would require that?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you said when you looked at these documents that there are two documents missing from the case history. Can you please tell us what is the first document that is missing from the case history? Please just give us the name of the document.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Reports on hospitalisation. That cannot be here. They are given when a patient is discharged. Then it is certified, then the bill for treatment, and then the patient goes home, and he no longer has this ID number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the two documents are the hospital history and the bill for payment; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
