utterances.text: The hospital history, does that include a chronology of the patient's hospitalisation in Uzice? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. It's a bill for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Tomasevic, when Mr. Groome asked you about the way in which entries are made in this protocol and the script that you used, that is the Cyrillic script, can you tell the Court - that may not be quite clear to everyone here - which are the scripts in use in Serbia and were in use in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The Cyrillic script. Some people also used the Latin script. It was not compulsory, either. It depended on the person. I prefer to write in Cyrillic. We were not obliged to write in either. It was up to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So both the Cyrillic and the Latin script were quite acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When Mr. Groome asked you whether you knew that Mr. Vasiljevic was tied upon admission, you said that you weren't working that day because it was a holiday but that your colleague who was present told you that he had been tied up.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In view of what you have just read, this information about the behaviour of the patient on the 7th of July, would that justify, on the basis of your own experience, the tying up of such a patient when he's brought to your department?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would justify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of that colleague who was working at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Shall I tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Stana Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you were giving us information about your own career, you told us that you have been working ever since 1979 continuously, but in answer to a question from Mr. Groome, you referred to a period when you attended this higher school in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tell us when it was that you were absent from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: That was in October. I wasn't absent throughout the year. I may have been absent for a month and then I'd come back to the ward, because I was going through advanced training parallel with work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you said October, what year were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In answer to another question from Mr. Groome, you explained that you entered the other information except diagnosis. I think that's what you said also in answer to my question, but you did say that there was something else that you didn't fill in with respect to Mitar Vasiljevic that you didn't mention just now. So my question is: Did you leave that out or did I misunderstand you? I think that you said, in answer to my question, that you didn't fill in the date of discharge.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I did not fill in the date the patient was discharged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So what you told me the first time was correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please madam, just pause before you answer. Remember you are both speaking the same language and the interpreters can't keep up unless you pause after the question before you begin your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, in answer to a question by Mr. Groome about abstinence, whether you may have noticed the effects of abstinence in Mr. Vasiljevic, you said, "I don't remember that." I want to make it clear. Do you mean that you don't remember the details of his disease and treatment or do you not remember just this particular detail?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: This particular detail. And it's a question that -- it's not up to me to answer such questions. I'm not the right person to answer such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It seems to me, Mrs. Tomasevic, that you didn't recollect many details and that's why I asked you this. Do you remember any other detail that might be of relevance?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just one more question for you, Mrs. Tomasevic. Do you personally remember that the period prior to 1992, do you remember Mitar Vasiljevic ever being a patient in your hospital ward?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Madam Tomasevic, you testified to the question by Mr. Domazet that one of the reasons you knew Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic fell off a horse was that Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic had a plaster cast on his leg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You mean that Mitar Vasiljevic had had a plaster cast already when he was transferred to the psychiatric ward from the orthopaedic ward?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I remember him having a plaster cast on his leg, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: When he was transferred to the psychiatric ward? I'll repeat my question. You remember that Mitar Vasiljevic had already a plaster cast when he was transferred to the psychiatric ward from the orthopaedic ward?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: When I saw him, he did have a plaster cast on his leg, yes. And in the course of treatment, in the course of treatment, I remember seeing it, in the course of his lying in hospital, in my ward. I remember seeing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: But you saw Mitar Vasiljevic with the plaster cast from the beginning when he was transferred to the psychiatric ward?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I remember that he had a plaster cast on his leg while he was lying in the psychiatric ward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: From the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that, but I do know that he had a plaster cast on his leg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do either counsel want to ask any questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: I have another question. Another question is: Please look at Exhibit 138 once more. The first page of Exhibit 138 shows a format of case history of the orthopaedic hospital, which is of Mitar Vasiljevic. This format has not changed from 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: You mean whether it's still like this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: My next question is also concerning Exhibit 138. On page 1 of Exhibit 138, column 17, which concerns the doctor who treated the patient. It is written, "Dr. B. Jovacevic and Dr. S. Simic." And page 4, there are names of Dr. Stojkovic and the name of Dr. Morjevic. On page 2, there is the name of Dr. Gordic. He is a surgeon. There is no name Dr. S. Simic except column 17 on page 1. Can you explain why the name of Dr. S. Simic is written in column 17?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Because Dr. Simic treated him in the psychiatric ward. Dr. Jovacecic was in the orthopaedic ward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do either counsel want to ask any questions arising out of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I have some, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomasevic, to this question by Judge Taya, you said that Dr. Simic was the neuropsychiatric physician and that he treated him and that's why his name is down there. Take a look, please, at the names that appear on page 3, the doctors on page 3. Or maybe it's 4 with the dates the 5th of July, the 7th of July, the 17th of July, that page. Which of these doctors are from the orthopaedics ward and which ones are possibly from the neuropsychiatric ward?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The 5th of July, 1992, Dr. Stojkovic, he's an orthopaedics surgeon. At 2200 hours, Dr. Stojkovic, orthopaedics surgeon. The 7th of July, Dr. Stojkovic, orthopaedics, and on the 17th, Dr. Bogdanovic, the late Dr. Bogdanovic, a neuropsychiatrist, and on the 17th of July, Dr. Moljevic, an orthopaedic surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So of these doctors, only on the 7th of July was the psychiatric doctor, and you recognised, I think, the handwriting of Dr. Bogdanovic a moment ago and recognised that he wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know why on the 7th of July, on that particular day, it wasn't Dr. Simic who examined the patient and gave his opinion but why it was Dr. Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: He was doing specialist training and he received the case history the next day. And he had his mentor, so they can't work themselves if they are doing specialist training. He had a mentor and that was Dr. Jevtovic, a lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you said he was a specialist trainee, which doctor do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I was thinking of Dr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the 7th of July you said was a national holiday. Were the duty doctors on duty or the doctors working generally?

utterances.speaker: MILENA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. It was just the doctor on duty who was working on the national holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, madam, for coming to give evidence and for the evidence you have given. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for listening to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, while we're waiting for the next witness, you are to tell us today the periods in those documents you wanted to be the subject of a forensic documentary examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise to the Court. I haven't had an opportunity to look at these books yet. I'm hoping that I can perhaps get them this evening or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Any exhibits you take away we'd like a receipt for, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Surely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Including the handwriting one which no doubt you've spirited away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not in possession of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Aren't you yet? Anyway, you may have access to them, but please just give us a receipt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, sir, will you please make the solemn declaration in the document which the court usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm going to be questioning you today, Mr. Simic, on behalf of the Defence team, and I kindly ask you to answer but to make pauses between my questions and your answer, because we speak the same language, but this will facilitate the work of the interpreters if we make a break. So please bear that in mind. Thank you. First of all, give us your name and surname, date of birth, and place of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: My name is Slobodan Simic. I was born in Uzice, Republic of Serbia, Yugoslavia. I was born on the 22nd of August, 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, what education have you had and when did you complete your education?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of medicine in Belgrade and I passed my specialist training in the field of psychiatry and now I am a specialist, a psychiatrist specialist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When did you graduate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I graduated in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What was your first job after graduation, Mr. Simic, your first place of employ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: My first job was in the general hospital of Uzice, in the psychiatric ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When did you start working on that ward?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I started working in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From 1991 onwards, how long did you work at the psychiatric ward of the Uzice hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I worked in the psychiatric ward until I left to do my specialist training in Belgrade, which was until 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After you finished your specialist training, did you go back to work in Uzice? And if not, where did you work after that and where do you work now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: After I finished my specialist training, I worked for six months in the general hospital in Uzice, and afterwards, I moved to Belgrade, and I worked for one and a half years in the prison hospital in Belgrade. After that, I returned to the Uzice general hospital, where I worked for about two years until three months ago, in fact, when I transferred to the clinical hospital centre called Zezdora [phoen] In Belgrade, which is somewhere I work now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, in mid-1992, where were you working, at what post in the Uzice hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I was working in the psychiatric ward of the Uzice general hospital as a general practitioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How many other doctors did the ward have, if you remember, and who were they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, the head of the ward was Dr. Borislav Martinovic, and the other doctors working there were Dr. Slavica Jelkovic, a lady doctor, and she was my mentor. Then there was Dr. Radoslava Bukovic, also a lady, and Dr. Zoran Dimitrijevic. As far as I remember, that was the team of psychiatrists working on the ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say, Mr. Simic, that Mrs. Slavica Jeftovic - not Jelkovic, Jeftovic - was your mentor, what do that mean in your life of work?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It meant that I was responsible for my work to her, which meant that all decisions having to do with patients directly were made by her. She made the decisions and I tabled the proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At that time, did the hospital have an organisation according to which there was an outpatient psychiatric department and a psychiatric ward?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was always an outpatient psychiatric department and the psychiatric ward proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you work on the ward?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I was what was called a ward doctor, which meant that I just worked on the ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From what you have told us, it transpires that you were a young doctor or starting out your training and career. You probably remember the method of organisation and method of work. What can you tell us, please? How were patients admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, there has been no challenge to what we have heard from the other doctors about this. Do you need to repeat it? As I understand it, this witness is here to establish that your client was in hospital, and if necessary, his psychiatric condition. That's all that you need to ask him about. None of this has been challenged. You are entitled to proceed on the basis that the Prosecution does not challenge it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not quite sure from Mr. Groome's questions, that is to say, I came to understand that the questions that he asked the previous witness expressed some doubt as to how the protocols were kept and how the patients were admitted into hospital. So I thought I would ask this witness about that procedure. If you consider that that is not necessary and that the matter is clear, I shall be happy to proceed and move on to asking the witness questions within the realm of his work as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: My clear understanding of the cross-examination, and if I'm wrong I better be set right, was that there was no challenge to the method by which these records were kept. The challenge was to whether that method was followed on this particular occasion by that particular witness and whether it was her writing on the document, and no more. But method, the general method that is meant to be followed, as I understand it, is not challenged. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Is that so, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So let's deal with what this witness is brought here for.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you happen to recall that during that period of time, and we're talking about 1992, that is to say, the second year in which you were working at the psychiatric ward of the general hospital, meeting a patient by the name of Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you remember and whether you, yourself, were his ward doctor? Because you said a moment ago that you were the ward doctor, or did you just take part in his treatment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I was the ward doctor of a patient Vasiljevic. It was my task, as the youngest doctor on the ward, to take care of the newly admitted patients, and in this case it was Mitar Vasiljevic. And that meant that I should check his state of health and to keep a record of his state of health in the case history, and also to inform my mentor regularly of the state of the patient's health.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Simic, any details, starting with the arrival of Mitar Vasiljevic on the ward and after that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I remembered the patient because he -- it is not usual or very frequent that patients are transferred from another ward in a psychotic state, a state of psychotic disturbance, so that I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From what ward was Mr. Mitar transferred to your ward, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Patient Mitar Vasiljevic was transferred from the orthopaedics ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember why he was in the orthopedics ward in the first place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: He was in a plaster cast so that it was the result of a fracture, most probably of the leg. And I think that's what was written in his case history, because the case history is the same one, common. It's just a continuation. It's taken over from the orthopedics ward. We continued writing in the case history when he came to our ward, and I think all that was recorded in his case history.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. That's as far as orthopedics is concerned. Now, the reason that he was transferred to the psychiatric ward, do you happen to remember that, the reasons for that and can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: The patient Vasiljevic was highly agitated, aggressive, and he was forcibly transferred to the psychiatric ward, so that on the ward we had to fixate or tie the patient and administer urgent therapy prescribed for that kind of condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember those first days or, rather, were you there when he was admitted or did you come in later? Did you find him on the ward when you came in later perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: He was brought to the ward, I assume on orders from one of the consultant psychiatrists who had probably examined him. I don't know that for sure, but the procedure is the psychiatric consultant examines the patient, and if he deems that the condition is such that he should be admitted to the psychiatric ward, then he is transferred to the ward. So I saw him when he had already been brought to the ward. And the man had the manifestations of acute psychotic disorder and therefore had to be tied.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you explain what that means in practical terms? You used the word "fix" or "fixated." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It means to be tied to the bed with special straps for protection, for the patient's own protection and to protect the staff as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say for the patient's and staff's protection, do you mean other patients, including the man himself?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The patient himself and other patients, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Simic, that if the doctors decide to strap the patient to the bed, that that means that the patient might be harmful to himself, that he might do something to harm his own person?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: A patient suffering from acute psychotic disorder is most often extremely agitated, excited, cannot control his behaviour. He is aggressive from time to time, and in a condition of that kind, because of the disorder that he is suffering from, he may hurt himself accidentally or hurt someone around him, and therefore, strapping him to the bed is a protective measure to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you happen to recall how long this protective measure was in place? How long was it applied for or how long is it generally applied for? Are there any hard and fast rules or is it individual, depending on the patient?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, it's an individual thing and depends on the psychological state of the patient in question. But in practice, generally speaking, it is a relatively short period of time, perhaps one or two days, until the initial surge of agitation and excitation passes and until the therapy and medicaments start working. So this condition is resolved fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say, Mr. Simic, under the effects of therapy, adequate therapy, medicaments, are strong medicaments administered which would have calming effects, artificial calming effects on the patient? Is that what you do? Is that the therapy?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, they are standard anti-psychotic drugs that we administer, drugs which affect sedation and lead to a calming effect of the -- and psycho-motor agitation and excitation, and they are customary and standardised procedure and a standard drug that is administered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll resume again tomorrow at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of November, 2001, at 9.30 a.m.
